g.text: 2 · Queue, take writeMu, write the group
3 · WAL APPEND — the commit point (under writeMu)

div.p: Under SyncAlways, "returned nil" means durable — for every record of a batch. Under SyncInterval / SyncNever an acknowledged write may still sit in the user-space buffer, so a process crash loses it too, not just power loss. A documented choice (see docs/DURABILITY.md), never the default.

g.text: 4 · Apply — under applyMu (exclusive), still under writeMu

div.p: Readers never take writeMu, so they never wait on the fsync. A search waits at most for one apply — one group of a batch — which is what the graph's own write lock already costs it.

g.text: 6 · Ack — mark every request in the group done, release writeMu

div.p: Before the append returns → no ack was given. A torn tail fails its checksum; replay truncates that segment logically at the tear and moves on. The write never happened.
After the append, before step 6 → the record is in the log (under SyncAlways, on disk). Replay re-applies it. A client retry is harmless: PUT is an upsert, and an unchanged vector costs nothing.
Index error after a durable append → the call fails, but the record replays on the next start. Log and index disagree until then — the direction the ordering rule chooses on purpose.
AddBatch failing midway → a durable prefix may exist; the DB is read-only, and the next start replays that prefix.

id: non-empty, ≤ 512 B, valid UTF-8 values: exactly the dimension fixed at Open — every one finite (NaN / ±Inf refused) metadata: ≤ 256 keys, string · bool · int64 · float64 AddBatch: ≤ 10,000, all checked before any is logged (defaults; WithLimits raises them up to hard ceilings)

Queue a putRequest, then take writeMu. Whoever holds it writes every queued request as one group (FIFO, ≤ maxBatch vectors, never splitting one) — a caller whose request was written meanwhile just returns its result. One group at a time across append and apply, so apply order is log order. Closed, WithReadOnly, or a past durability failure → refused.

g.text: one vector → applyPut · a group → applyPuts
4a · Is this id already live? — the upsert branch (g.mu held)

p.strong: Why not just overwrite node.vector in place?

div.p: The slot's index is referenced by neighbor lists all over the graph, and those edges were chosen for the OLD vector — they claim "these two are close" about a pair that no longer is. Searches would keep being routed in from a region the vector has left.

Repairing them is not available either: pruning makes edges asymmetric, so a node's own neighbor list is not the list of nodes pointing at it. Finding every inbound edge means scanning the whole graph, O(N·M) per update.
A fresh slot is correct by construction. It costs one dead slot — the same debt Delete takes on, paid to Compact.

g.text: link() — for each layer min(level, maxLevel) → 0
InsertBatch — per group, in chunks of 4 × workers

div.p: Non-blocking send on a 1-slot channel, only when the live count has doubled or halved. The calibrator runs in its own goroutine.
[crc32c][type=PUT][seq][len] — 17 B header payload = [version][idLen][id][dim][float32s][meta] crc covers type, seq and len, not just payload seq assigned by the writer — strictly increasing
User space, not the kernel. Rotates at MaxSegmentBytes, fsyncing the old segment first. A group streams its n records through the same buffer.

SyncAlways (zero value) — fsync before return, ~4.24 ms A group — one batch, or many writers' Adds — pays one fsync SyncInterval — ticker fsyncs every 50 ms (default) SyncNever — ~780 ns; flushed when the buffer fills or on Close
Sticky: the DB is permanently ErrReadOnly, reads keep working. Emits DurabilityFailure (under writeMu — the observer must not call back).

One hold of applyMu covers index.Insert and store.Put, so no reader sees (v2, md1). A batch keeps the last occurrence of each id and applies in groups of applyGroup = max(64, 4 × workers), releasing applyMu between groups.
Copies so the graph never aliases a caller buffer. Normalizes for Cosine. Done outside the graph's lock: it touches only the caller's slice and config.

g.text: ids[id] hit, same vector → return nil
ids[id] hit, new vector → tombstone the old slot

div.p: int(-log(rand) * ml), ml = 1/ln(M) Seeded RNG; a serial build is reproducible, a parallel batch is not (WithInsertWorkers(1)). A replacement draws a fresh level.

g.text: ef=1, just to find a good entry point

ol.li: searchLayer(vec, cur, EfConstruction, lc, nil) — a build never filters
pruneConnections — trim to cap, demoting tombstones
seed next layer with the closest hit

div.p: Each chunk holds g.mu throughout; readers get it back between. Workers = min(workers, live / 32) — a small graph grows serially.

ol.li: serial: upsert rule, randomLevel in batch order, place
a node above maxLevel is linked alone → entry fixed
parallel link(): striped nodeLocks (4,096 · 32 KiB), never two held; node.linking hides in-flight nodes from other workers' traversals

div.p: In-RAM store.Map, keys and strings interned. Durable only through the WAL record and the snapshot's second section — no payload file.
slices.Equal against the stored form. No tombstone, no slot, no edge touched.

This is the WAL-replay path: recovery re-applies records the graph already holds across a snapshot boundary, and if that cost a slot every restart would inflate the graph with tombstones. ~331 ns, against 776 µs for a real replacement.

ol.li: node.deleted = true — the slot stays, keeping its index and every edge it has
was this slot the entry? → reelectEntry(), or the descent below starts from a corpse

div.p: Inside Insert's own write lock, never by calling Delete — that would open a window where the id belongs to nobody, and a reader would observe an update as a disappearance.

unchanged → graph untouched, metadata still written
